item.title: A Circularity at the Heart of Safety Assurance
item.description:
A friend of yours says they've had a flash of insight. A manga they've been into lately has helped them understand something deep and fundamental about decision theory. You aren't yet clear on the details when they rush off to work on "practical applications", but before long they return with their magnum opus:

"This hard drive contains the weights of an AI model that is both wildly superintelligent and completely safe!"

You feel as though you have good reasons to be pretty skeptical of this claim. This friend has terrible taste in manga, and you aren't convinced that they grasp the more subtle themes in the stuff they do read. You're about to shoo them away when, anticipating a dismissal, your friend pleads:

"What would convince you that I'm right?"

Now, if this friend wanted to convince you that they were wearing the Crunchyroll Store exclusive Solo Leveling Beru Tee, you could verify that claim directly, with the unaided senses. It's as simple as taking a look at their outfit. Assessing the safety of the AI model is not so simple. Observations of the hard drive are separated from the fact you want to know by a gulf of empirical and logical uncertainty. Whether or not the model is safe is dependent on the unpredictable behaviours produced by the model weights, and on the environment's responses to those behaviours. Since the AI model and the environment around it are so complex, we cannot anticipate the relevant dimensions of these phenomena without some kind of instrument that aids us in interpreting our observations. Without such an instrument, I would consider safety to be an unobservable variable.

You could ask your friend to provide you with an instrument that could be used to measure the AI model's safety. Maybe, this instrument is a safety case, where claims are written in natural language and presented diagrammatically. Or, maybe it ends up looking like a mathematical proof, formalised in Lean. In any case, the instrument is based on some theory that relates safety to variables that you can observe.

Suppose you make that request, though, and your friend comes back at you with this:

Well, that wasn't very convincing. Whatever theory this safety case is based on is clearly no good. But presumably your friend disagrees, or they wouldn't have shown it to you in the first place. How can you come to agree on which instruments are valid? Either one of you could appeal to some a priori arguments, and those arguments may allow you to dismiss some incoherent theories, but what you're left with could still be an inaccurate reflection of reality. At some point then, you must demand that your friend validates their instrument empirically. They should use it to make predictions about the real world, and show that those predictions are accurate.

Your friend cannot satisfy this demand though, even in principle. How can they show that their instrument makes predictions that match our observations, when we aren't yet able to make those observations without first having a valid instrument? This is the circularity that lies at the heart of safety assurance.

We could try to get around this circularity by validating this theory on the basis of other stuff that it predicts. But the theory could easily predict other stuff well, while nevertheless being wrong about safety. Alternatively, we could try to validate the instrument's ability to predict safety in conditions where we're confident in our judgements about safety. For example, the instrument should tell us that a GPT-2 instance running in a sandbox is safe, whereas a GPT-2 instance hooked up to the actuators in an autonomous vehicle is not safe. But how do we justify the assumption that the instrument's validity generalises from these conditions to the conditions we actually care about?

Throughout the history of science, this same circularity has come up again and again. How can you validate a thermometer without already being able to measure temperature? And how can you validate a clock without first being able to measure time? Hasok Chang calls it The Problem of Nomic Measurement, and Bas Van Fraassen (following Reichenbach) refers to it as The Problem of Coordination. However, we're lucky to live in a world where we have clocks and thermometers that we can rely on, so how was this circularity addressed in those cases?

This is the question that Chang explores in Inventing Temperature. He finds that scientists often begin with a plausible, but flawed, starting point. In the case of temperature, this starting point was our own sensory perception of hot and cold. We build our first instruments on this basis, and then use those instruments to scrutinise the thing we started with. For example: we notice that the expansion of mercury correlates with our sensory perception of hot and cold, we build thermometers out of mercury, and then find that the mercury thermometer is actually more consistent than our own senses. Chang refers to this process as self-correction. Instruments can be improved in other ways too, which Chang refers to collectively as enrichment. For example: we can calibrate the mercury thermometer against conditions that are relatively easy to reproduce – like the boiling and freezing points of water – in order to ensure that readings are consistent between thermometers. Chang calls this whole process – establishing and improving instruments through self-correction and enrichment – epistemic iteration.

So, can we establish an instrument for assessing the safety of a superintelligent AI model through epistemic iteration? Would such an instrument do what we want it to do, and what would the process of developing it look like? It seems as though epistemic iteration has produced reliable instruments in the past, but there are many disanalogies between AI safety and thermometry. The failure of a thermometer to function as intended can reveal new insights that can be leveraged to build better thermometers, whereas failures in safety assurance might not be survivable. Also, a superintelligent AI model can adapt to the instruments applied to it in a way that mercury cannot.

Right now, my best answer to your friend's question – "What would convince you that I'm right?" – is that I want a rigorous safety case, with mathematical guarantees wherever possible, built on top of frameworks that have worked well in other industries, and stress-tested by well-resourced independent experts. However, I don't think that's a good enough answer. Expert judgment is fallible, and when the stakes are so high, I want standards built upon a sturdier foundation.

item.title: My Paranoid Coding Machine Setup
item.description:
The combination of running AI agents which can install and run anything with supply chain attacks / the Hackening has made me much more paranoid about my personal machine than I used to be. I've been slowly improving this, and finally moved all of my AI agents into a VM today. I'm sharing this to show how far you can take this, even if you have requirements like GPU access or the ability to run (something close enough to) Docker.

This is a follow-up / longer version of a recent shortform.

Goals

I run Claude Code in a custom harness which currently disables all permission prompts. I'm not really that worried about Claude doing something dangerous on purpose, but I worry about:

  • Claude breaking something by accident (mistyping a command that turns into rm -rf /).
  • Claude installing malware (most likely via a supply chain attack).

My biggest worry is kernel exploits giving attackers access to my user account, allowing them to install a keylogger and steal my password manager vault[1].

Claude needs the ability to run Docker for testing, and shared access to my GPU for ML work.

Non-Goals

To get its work done, Claude needs access to many API keys (GitHub, OpenRouter, etc.). These keys are already as limited as they can be, and I limit the amount of API credits each key can access anyway because Claude doesn't understand the value of money.

Agent VM

I moved Claude agents to an unprivileged user account inside of an unprivileged VM. Any user that can run Docker can easily get root access (and root access within the VM makes sandbox escape much easier) so agents use rootless Podman instead.

GPU drivers allow direct access to hardware, and assigning the GPU to a VM would prevent my computer from being used by humans, so the VM can't access the GPU directly.

GPU Container

For GPU usage, agents use my GPU queueing tool over SSH into an unprivileged container using gVisor + nvproxy. This has an allowlist for Nvidia driver calls, which reduces the attack surface for driver exploits (although imperfectly).

Production TTS Containers

I run a Text-to-Speech service for my RSS reader on this machine, since everything commercially available is either weirdly slow[2] or ridiculously expensive. I decided to run Kokoro-82M locally, but didn't want to expose a service containing C code[3] to the internet. I had Claude rewrite the C code in Rust, and (just in case) heavily sandbox the code with GPU access:

The only port opened to the internet (via Cloudflare Tunnel[4]) is written entirely in Rust and has no privileges or GPU access. It talks to a separate container with GPU access (through gVisor + nvproxy, like my other GPU container) over a very simple binary protocol where the only inputs are tokenized phonemes (a list of numbers).

I'm still unsure if this piece is sufficiently paranoid, but I really like having fast TTS and don't want to spend $200+/mo for a cloud GPU (or to send my users' data to other people's gaming machines).

Gotchas

Segfaults in the agent VM

This may have something to do with faulty hardware on my machine[5], but switching from host-passthrough to host-model in libvirt fixed it for me.

File descriptor leak in gVisor with directfs=false

I was using this to avoid running the sandbox as root. Moving the GPU container to rootless Podman with directfs worked instead.

Other Security Hardening

  • Kernel updates are applied without restarting via Ubuntu Pro / Livepatch (free for up to 5 machines, although the agent VM counts for one).
  • Secure Boot is enabled, using Canonical's signed driver modules.
  • Several unused kernel modules are disabled, especially network protocols that I don't use (sctp, rds, tipc and n_hdlc).
  • I removed my own account from the docker group to limit malware's impact on my own account, although a keylogger could still get past this.
  • A firewall blocks all inbound requests except via Tailscale, and my Tailscale policy is fairly locked-down now: My personal devices can access each other via advertised services and (key-only) SSH; the agent VM can only access the TTS service.
  • Package managers proxy installs through Socket Firewall (free), which warns or blocks known malware in packages.

Next Steps

The biggest remaining security improvement for me is probably running every application in a separate VM, or at least running my browser in a VM (although I already use the Snap version of Firefox, which does some sandboxing).

I'm also slightly worried about Canonical or another vendor I depend on getting hacked and putting malware in the official repos. I haven't figured out how to mitigate this yet.

Summary

If you're sufficiently paranoid, it's possible to have AI agents running on your machine while sandboxing them to a pretty acceptable level, even if they need GPU access and tools like Docker.

  1. ^

    I intentionally don't keep 2FA keys in my password manager vault, so this wouldn't be entirely catastrophic, but most of my accounts don't use 2FA and it would still be very annoying to change hundreds of passwords.

  2. ^

    OpenRouter claims that Kokoro-82M's latency is <300 ms, but in practice I was seeing several seconds, especially for longer inputs. My local machine using a low-end previous generation GPU responds in ~50 ms and processes at 200x realtime.

  3. ^

    espeak-ng CVEs that haven't been fixed in a released version: CVE-2023-49990, CVE-2023-49991, CVE-2023-49992, CVE-2023-49993.

  4. ^

    I chose Cloudflare Tunnel over Tailscale Funnel because it adds additional protections in front of your service, including an API key handled by Cloudflare before hitting a second API key handled by my service.

  5. ^

    My CPU is known to be flaky in some situations.

item.title: "Hardwired Pause" should likely be your favorite (pause) plan.
item.description:
I'm part of a team of 26 researchers that recently released a 212-page paper proposing a new plan for pausing AI, the "hardwired pause."[1] The paper is called "The Feasibility of a Hardwired Pause of Frontier AI Training." Our analysis suggests that, under this hardwired pause plan, we could probably pause for at least a decade if we start stopping within the next year, and this could likely be extended indefinitely. I expect this to be possible without trusting China or tanking the economy.

Note: I am speaking for myself and not the other 25 authors. The working group is led by Will Fithian and Wesley Holliday, and the work continues.

I currently think:

  1. The best plan is to pause/stop AI, i.e. have an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development. And importantly, this is technically easier than more nuanced international regulation.
  2. A hardwired pause is probably the best plan out there for how to do this (except maybe it doesn't go far enough).
  3. This paper is likely the most in-depth analysis of pause feasibility in existence.

Discussion and disagreement on any of these is very welcome!

What's a hardwired pause?

A hardwired pause basically means:

  1. Stop making chips that can be used to train new AI models.
  2. Only make chips that can only be used to run inference on existing AI models (or that aren't AI accelerators at all). We call these "inference-only chips"; I'm also calling them "hardwired chips."

This is an instance of an "inference-only" pause, which others have previously proposed.

The main advantage hardwired chips provide is making the pause robust and durable. With other approaches to inference-only pauses, because training-capable chips are still being produced, it would be somewhat easier to build a secret fleet of them, and potentially much easier to rapidly resume a race to superintelligence (if you could seize a large fraction of the governed training-capable chips).

I think any credible pause plan must account for and govern existing chips. Our work also includes an in-depth analysis of how a "chip census" might proceed, and expect all but ~10,000 of the US's ~30,000,000 and China's ~3,000,000 "H100-equivalents" would likely be recoverable.[2]

In a hardwired pause, these chips could initially be transitioned to inference, verified with other techniques, before being decomissioned once hardwired chips are available. Of course, chips could also be governed in other ways, e.g. decomissioned, and the total number of hardwired chips produced could also be controlled... in general, there are many design-choices in the space of hardwired pauses available to policy-makers.


Why is this better than Plan A?

Epistemic Status: I have skimmed much of Plan A, discussed it with authors for >1 hour, and seen a presentation about it prior to its release.

In my mind, Plan A and a Hardwired Pause both start with a chip census and preventing further development until a more durable arrangement is reached. But instead of phasing out training chips for hardwired chips, Plan A relies on continued verification by other means to try to do the following for a duration of roughly 15 years:

The key disadvantage of Plan A I see is the "dry tinder problem": with all of this training-capable compute lying around, if the race resumes for some reason, it could take a very short period of time (e.g. days-to-months) to achieve superintelligence. Plan A tries to mitigate this by making the datacenters easy to destroy (e.g. Chinese datacenters are in Canada). But this still seems likely to be destabilizing, since the datacenters could be destroyed for reasons other than "you defected on the treaty." This makes it riskier to rely on them for things that are critical to national security, but it seems like AI will likely become critical to those things in Plan A.

The main advantage of Plan A I see is that it may in fact not be possible to have an extremely durable pause, especially with algorithmic progress. But I tend to think that for now, we should just be focused on continuously improving our ability to robustly maintain a pause, and that it is premature to assume a pause would need to end before long.

How is this different from MIRI's Plan S?

Epistemic Status: I have read AI Futures Project's short description of Plan S. I have skimmed but not read MIRI's "An International Agreement to Prevent the Premature Creation of Artificial Superintelligence," which I take to be the most detailed version of the plan, but I have discussed them with MIRI's technical governance team for >1 hour. This plan aims to stop AI progress indefinitely using a variety of conventional verification and enforcement methods:

A Hardwired Pause could be viewed as a particular instance of Plan S that differs from MIRI's in the details, specifically:

  1. MIRI's paper doesn't propose a specific verification mechanism, whereas we propose hardwired chips. I currently think the use of hardwired chips is basically a strict upgrade over alternative approaches to verification that don't get rid of training-capable chips,[3] and therefore have a potential dry tinder problem.
  2. MIRI's paper also includes research restrictions. These restrictions and other enforcement mechanisms involved in their plan might be more intrusive and carry greater concerns around civil liberties and concentration of power. Research restrictions are less important with hardwired chips, since they would not be able to run unapproved models. But research is still not without risks!

What are my biggest concerns about a hardwired pause (vs. getting rid of chips entirely)?

I've previously proposed systematically dismantling the compute supply chain, which is basically a hardwired pause without the hardwired inference chips. I think the hardwired pause proposal in our paper may not go far enough, especially if it is implemented too late. Some specific concerns are:

  1. The infrastructure needed to produce hardwired chips is probably quite similar to that needed to produce training-capable chips, so the hardwired pause still provides a much better starting point for a resumed race.
  2. There may be too much algorithmic progress.[4] Specifically, I think of three failure modes, all of which more advanced AI models could help contribute to via AI R&D:
    1. Techniques that dramatically reduce the compute or communication bandwidth needed for training.
    2. Advances in computing hardware.
    3. New AI or computing paradigms that are dramatically more efficient.
    4. A "scaffolding singularity" in which ever more powerful AI is built using existing models as merely one component in a larger system.
  3. Setting aside the above concerns, I'm still very uncertain whether existing models are, or will be, net positive for society.

On the other hand, I see two main advantages of a hardwired pause:

  1. Defection on the pause is less tantalizing. Instead of becoming the only one with powerful AI, you are still up against a bunch of hardwired AI models and so the relative gains you can expect from building a more powerful frontier in violation of the agreement are smaller.
  2. Existing AI systems might help improve the stability of the pause, or otherwise help us make use of a pause (e.g. to do more safety research, or improve collective sense-making and decision-making).

Overall, I'm still inclined to favor the "get rid of the compute plan", while recognizing that the hardwired pause might be much, MUCH more palatable to many actors. Within AI Safety in particular, my sense is that people usually have lower p(doom) than me, usually have more specific and limited concerns about AI than I do, and often value the existence of current AI systems highly. Thus I think, if you are reading this, a hardwired pause should likely be your favorite (pause) plan, as per the title.

Why is the paper so long? What's in it?

The paper includes a reasonably fleshed out example of a hardwired pause, but most of the space is what I believe is the most in-depth analysis of feasibility that's been published. So arguably the main contribution is not the idea of a hardwired pause, but this analysis of feasibility.

In this work, feasibility encompasses durability, palatability, and reliability. And it touches on not just technical, but also political, geopolitical, and economic aspects of feasibility. The main questions regarding feasibility (and my brief answers) include:

  1. Can you actually make chips that are only useful for running existing models?
    1. Strong yes, we have a decent proof-of-concept from Taalas.
  2. Can you find enough of the existing chip supply to prevent secret projects?
    1. Quite likely yes, assuming pause-willingness and no algorithmic breakthroughs. AI chips are expensive capital goods that leave copious paper trails when they're built, purchased, operated, and (if they fail) returned under warranty. In particular, companies in both the U.S. and China get tax writeoffs for telling the government about them when they're purchased, and this applies even to chips smuggled into China.
  3. Can you monitor fabs reliably enough to ensure that appreciable quantities of chips are not being produced in secret?
    1. Quite likely yes. The supply chain is very complicated and would be difficult to replicate secretly; fabs need regular maintenance and produce signature chemical residues; and the location of relevant machines seems to be known.
  4. Would this crash the economy?
    1. There would probably be some economic impact, but much less than the 2008 financial crisis, e.g. it might decrease growth by 25% (vs. leading to negative growth for ~2 years in the case of the 2008 crisis).
    2. Two big points I want to emphasize:
      1. While some AI investments are heavily leveraged, the real economy is fairly insulated from these speculative investments.
      2. A big question is how much diffusion of models-existing-at-the-time-of-a-pause could support these investments; this seems plausible to me.
  5. How much would the U.S. and China need to trust each other for this to work?
    1. Not that much -- this plan is based on verification, not trust, and was developed with the advice of former diplomats with experience in arms control. A central objective of this plan is to give the U.S. and China confidence that nobody is continuing frontier AI development in secret, and that this state of affairs is robust and durable. In implementing a hardwired pause, they would need to cooperate quite a bit, but if they genuinely want an international pause, they would have good reason to do so. The main places I see trust coming in are:
      1. Trusting that purported pause-willingness is real and worth engaging with. Countries don't seriously risk being duped into unilaterally pausing, but policymakers might assume the other side is not engaging in good faith and not want to waste effort on an initiative they expect to fail.
      2. Extending trust may be useful in various small ways during the chip census. For instance, let's say the U.S. and China both have 100k chips unaccounted for, but would be able to find (or "find") an additional 90k chips with more effort. Then they can both benefit from cooperating further on the margin (e.g. "find" another 2k chips) in order to elicit further cooperation from the other side (who might then "find" another 2k chips), etc. But I expect this would be much faster and smoother with more mutual trust. Importantly, if either side is convinced the other side is refusing to cooperate, that could threaten the agreement, so if both sides in fact want the agreement to succeed more than they want to have a bit more dark compute, it seems like they should be able to find a way to cooperate, although there is still a bargaining problem here.

Conclusion

I was inspired to write this after realizing that this work hadn't been properly socialized within the AI Safety community. While admitting a bias towards thinking the things I work on are significant, I think this is among the most important pieces of work for this community. My hope is that it provides a definitive refutation of the claim that pausing is impossible, making it impossible for learned people to credibly make such arguments publicly.

At the same time, this is part of an ongoing effort, and is in some sense a work in progress. There are many questions I am interested in that deserve further investigation, and I am keen to hear your thoughts and know how it is landing with other audiences you present it to.

And Will and Wes are enthusiastic for further discussion and engagement as well! :)

  2. ^

    The exact number is hard to predict, of course, and would also depend on the level of international cooperation achieved (more on this at the end of the blog post).

  3. ^

    The main advantage I had seen for other verification approaches is that hardwired models might have issues that need patching, and this wouldn't be supported by hardwired chips. But apparently this is not true for all chip designs; I highly recommend checking out https://github.com/Berkeley-AI-Risk/inference-only to learn more about hardwired chip designs.

  4. ^

    Notably, the estimated rate of algorithmic progress in this work comes from Dwarkesh's blog and is lower than has been estimated by others, e.g. Aaron Scher from MIRI who pointed me to https://epochai.substack.com/p/the-least-understood-driver-of-ai as currently the best starting point reference on algorithmic progress. This is something I plan to look into more, but to summarize my current understanding: 1) Algorithmic changes may lead to greater returns with more compute, 2) Algorithmic progress behind the frontier can take advantage of models at the frontier (e.g. via distillation). Both of these factors suggest slower algorithmic progress during a hardwired pause: defectors would 1) be working with less compute and 2) be trying to advance the frontier, not playing catch up.

item.title: Would you press the button? The hard problem of alignment
item.description:
There is a TL;DR at the end.

The heaven button: You wake up one day and find a button in front of you, with a proof next to it. The proof says that pressing the button will kill everyone on the planet and send them all to heaven. Would you press it?

It seems too good to be true. You think it must be a dream. It can't possibly be true. You go through the proof, and it seems correct. But what if you were under the influence of some drug?

But the stakes are very high, so you use software you trust to formalize it in Lean, and you run it on a machine you trust. Lean says the proof is correct so now you are more convinced. But you start doubting yourself again. What if someone compromised the formalization software, or introduced a bug in Lean?

So you check Lean's code, and run the proof on a second machine with an independent checker. It passes again. But each of these checks could fail in the same way the first one could. So you go further and formally verify Lean and the formalization software themselves. They pass. But now you are doubtful of the tool you used to verify this. What if that was compromised by someone? Every new check needs another check behind it, and at some point you have to stop and decide.

Would you press it?

A common belief in AI labs and AI safety is that handing control to some general superintelligence would be fine, if we have a formal proof of alignment. That, in my opinion, is saying yes to the same button, except there is no proof yet, only the hope of one.

In this post, I present what I think is the hard problem of alignment.

  • First, I illustrate why testing for alignment is not enough and a proof would be required.
  • Then I lay out why a proof could be intractable.
  • Finally, I argue that even a formal proof that a superintelligence is aligned does not justify its development.

The hard problem of alignment

The hard problem of alignment: How can a system reliably establish whether a system broadly smarter than itself is aligned with it?

The main problem is that a failed test can sometimes show a system is misaligned, but passing every test does not establish that it is aligned.

Note: The question is not whether this is impossible. There may be systems smarter than us whose relative safety we can establish in some sense. The difficulty centres around two terms:

  • Broadly smarter: I mean smarter in general, as Eliezer Yudkowsky describes it,[1]and not just better at specific tasks like chess.
  • Reliably establish: I mean to a standard that fits the risk of an irreversible transfer of power, much higher than the one we use for most technologies.

Part 1: Merely testing can't establish alignment, you would have to prove it

We will use a simple framework to illustrate the difficulty. It is a bit reductive and not a proper formalism of alignment.

Say a system wants to check whether a system is aligned with it. Let be the set of all possible states of the world, and for a state , let be the action in that state that finds desirable. It could also stand for the action that is beneficial for humanity. Let be the action actually takes. For alignment, we would want something like:

With testing, we can only ever check finitely many states, a set . So what a test actually shows is:

It is roughly the state of the art in how frontier labs and many AI safety experts talk about alignment and decide whether it is getting better. A model's system card reports an "alignment assessment," a set of evaluations, and the model is judged against earlier models on how often it behaves badly in them.[2]

To go from to , we need to prove why the behavior should generalize to all states.

Why isn't induction enough? In most industries, it is often enough. We run safety tests and trials, and when a product passes enough of them, we trust it. But if is broadly smarter than , we have to take seriously the possibility that can pass every test can come up with, whether it is aligned or not. Models already sometimes recognize when they are being evaluated, and have behaved differently when they believed they were being trained.[2][3]So we can't rely on induction from to .

Such a proof could come from different places: formal methods, a deep understanding of how the system was trained, interpretability, and so on. We would need to establish holds outside .

Why such proofs could be intractable

1. is not resolved for all states. doesn't know what it wants in most states of the world. Humans disagree with each other and change our minds. So the right-hand side of the equation is not defined for most of .

2. can bring about states we can't reason about. Even if we try to resolve for every situation we can imagine, a system broadly smarter than us can bring about situations that are hard for us to imagine and reason about.

3. can manipulate the target. If can't be fixed in advance, it is open to manipulation. For new situations, what we want would have to be decided later, when they come up. But by then is part of the world we are deciding in, and it can shape what we want, changing the right-hand side instead of the left.

Proposals that try to get around

People have proposed different ways around not being resolved. Roughly, they either hand the job of working out to , or keep us as the judge.

  • Coherent extrapolated volition (CEV) lets the system work out what we would want if we knew more and were wiser.[4]
  • Corrigibility doesn't try to fix at all. It asks for a system that lets us correct it or shut it down.[5]
  • Debate has two systems argue and lets a human judge which one gave the most true and useful information.[6]

I don't think any of them resolve it.

With CEV, does the extrapolating. We could look at the procedure and test some of its outputs, but we are not the wiser, better-informed version of ourselves it is extrapolating to. The further the extrapolation departs from judgments we can make ourselves, the harder it is to establish that it is what we would have wanted, and not just something that looks plausible. So we are back to the problem in Part 1.

Corrigibility and debate keep us in the loop instead of fixing in advance. That helps, but it doesn't remove the problem. Corrigibility tries to make a system accept correction and shutdown without manipulating or resisting us, but the original paper did not fully solve how to do this.[5]Debate tries to help us judge questions we couldn't judge on our own, but it has unresolved problems,[7]and it can only settle the questions we think to ask. In both cases, our judgement is open to manipulation by , as in point 3.

Part 2: Even a proof can't justify superintelligence

Let's assume we get past all of this and have a proof that is aligned. We would still need to verify it. Let be an evaluator working in a formal framework , for example a world model, a safety specification and a verifier, as some guaranteed-safe AI proposals describe.[8]If checks and accepts it:

This is definitely an upgrade from tests, and it would give us considerable trust in . It is also how we already handle some of the highest-stakes systems we build, such as flight control software and secure operating systems, where formal verification is used to prove that the software does what its specification says.

But to reliably establish alignment, we would need a further guarantee that neither nor (nor ) was compromised by in a way that led to the verification passing.

But if we have proven that is aligned, doesn't that already rule this out? No. The passing of the proof was the verification, and we haven't established that the verification itself was intact. Using 's alignment to confirm the proof would be circular.

We can add another check on the evaluator to ensure this. Say checks the integrity of . If the check fails, we find out that something went wrong. But a pass does not rule out that could have been compromised too. So we might need to check , leading to an infinite regress:

Each guarantee needs another guarantee behind it, and there is no point where the chain establishes itself. This is the regress of doubts from the heaven button story, and it applies to basically any proof where we can’t establish or ensure a boundary between what is being checked and what is checking it.

So even with a formal proof, we still depend on the verification not having been compromised, and on the formal system matching the real world. If we can't establish either of these well enough, and being wrong could take away our ability to intervene, then the proof is not enough to justify handing over control.

Q: We base our lives on things without absolute guarantees all the time. With your reasoning, it sort of implies there is no such thing as an absolute guarantee, because this regress will apply to any proof.

We have mathematical proofs that hold up, and we use them in high-stakes scenarios. If we had a formal proof that a superintelligent system smarter and more powerful than any of us is aligned to us, why should we not take that?

I agree that there is a spectrum of certainty on which we base our lives. We trust engineers based on their calculations, vaccines based on trials, doctors to cut us open and operate, and our elected governments to make decisions for us.

We trust formal proofs for high-stakes situations. And yes, the regress applies to every proof. I think the question of where we stop checking depends on two things: the cost of being wrong, and whether there is reason to believe that what we are evaluating can influence or manipulate the evaluator. The consequences of a failure in other technologies, however serious, are relatively contained or reversible. So we accept a certain level of confidence and stop checking. A superintelligence, on the other hand, would be smarter than those evaluating it, and the consequences of getting it wrong could be catastrophic for everyone, with no possibility of reversing the outcome.

I am not questioning the validity of proofs within a formal system. I am pointing to the limitations of formalism when we try to apply it to the real world. Developing superintelligence could lead to irreversible consequences, and we can never have a guarantee that it won't. That alone should be the strongest argument against pursuing it.

Q: Are you saying that we should not build AI?

No. We should be building AI that makes us more productive, helps us solve hard problems, and moves science forward. I think we should build AI with a focus on amplifying humans,[9]and never, at any stage, let control slip from humanity on the assumption that alignment will save us.

We can have relative safety for systems that are better than us at specific tasks, which can be useful to humanity in many different domains. Formal proofs and deep understanding of the model can help us establish those claims. We might have to be careful about the boundary between evaluator and evaluatee.

But we would need to imagine a different way of developing AI rather than proceeding with the goal of developing broadly smarter intelligence and working backwards to solve alignment including hopes to find formal proofs of such. Such an approach is bad, as there will not be a complete guarantee that things won't go really bad for everyone.

Q: So should one press the button?

My claim is that whatever framework you use, morality, decision theory, rationality, or some other epistemic approach, it should ultimately lead you to conclude that pressing the button is not justified.

I am not an expert in these fields, but it is not a new problem, and several related lines of thought seem to point toward the same conclusion.

  • Maximin. Rawls argued that when probabilities can't be trusted, when little is lost by playing safe, and when the worst outcomes are unacceptable, it is rational to choose the option with the least bad worst case.[10]
  • Consent. The button decides for everyone, and not everyone agreed to it.
  • Flawed arguments. In high-stakes decisions, the chance that an argument itself is flawed can matter more than what it calculates.[11]
  • Corrupted hardware. Yudkowsky argued that we should not seize power even when it seems to benefit everyone, because our own reasoning might be compromised.[12]

To me, the fanaticism to build and hand off control to some superintelligence is uncomfortably close to that of an altruistic suicide bomber, who is so convinced by the payoff that they are willing to take a step that can't be undone.


TL;DR

Testing can show that a system is misaligned, but cannot establish that a broadly smarter system will remain aligned outside the situations we test. A formal proof would be much stronger evidence, but it could be intractable. And even a formal proof does not provide an absolute guarantee, as it does not guarantee the integrity of the proof, verifier, specification, and their connection to the real world. If those assumptions cannot themselves be adequately established, and failure could mean an irreversible loss of human control, then even formal verification is not enough to justify handing control to a superintelligence.

item.title: Whose Side? A game where you audit models for secret loyalties
item.description:
Try the app here: whoseside.web.app. You can chat with a model and try to work out which who it secretly favours.

With the recent Hugging Face attack, we're relying more and more on LLMs to audit the trails and safeguard the actions of other LLMs. That makes it vital to be sure our LLMs really are the helpful assistant they're presented ( as they can easily be sleeper agents.[1] ). We need a way to keep our agents working for us. Or at least a way to tell if it goes wrong.

Compared with buggy code, buggy AI is a lot harder to define or solve.[2] Mechanistic interpretability has some promising leads[3], but is still nowhere close to being able to point out novel misalignment. If we look at the field of cybersecurity, first a vulnerability comes out or an attacker discovers something new, and then defenses get built. I find that's a good analogy for machine learning as well, where we've seen this pattern with adversarial attacks on images and jailbreaking prompts. Currently, open-weight models offer no guarantee that they are helpful-only or aligned, besides our ability to evaluate them.[4] You're essentially trusting that nowhere in the model training supply chain has a vulnerability, bug, or secret loyalty been inserted or post-trained into the weights. Current sleeper-agent / secret-loyalty research says as much.[5]

[6]

To demonstrate this problem, I built a little website where you can try to audit and find the secret loyalties instilled into these models. For those familiar with the prompt-injection game Gandalf, this is a similar idea. Try it here: whoseside.web.app.[7]

The code is available at [repo link TODO]. This work was funded by a BlueDot Impact Rapid Grant.

item.title: 25% of People Have Avoidant Attachment (But It Can Be Healed!)
item.description:
Relationships are hard, but having an avoidant attachment makes relationships a hell of a lot harder.

Within attachment theory (which helps explain interpersonal bonding), it’s known that ~25% of the population uses avoidant attachment strategies to escape intimacy. Why? Because emotional intimacy and being vulnerable with a romantic partner causes them significant discomfort.

But why does it cause them discomfort? Prior experiences (usually stemming from childhood) instilled in them that their emotional needs would not be met by their primary caregivers. And when someone’s needs are repeatedly not met, they subconsciously suppress those needs rather than face the daily pain of rejection.

That learned strategy—to shut down when attempting to seek emotional intimacy—can persist long into adulthood.

Emotional loneliness is at the core of avoidant attachment

In the book Adult Children of Emotionally Immature Parents, the author explains that:

What happens when … immature parents lack the emotional responsiveness necessary to meet their children’s emotional needs? The result is emotional neglect.

Emotional neglect in childhood leads to painful emotional loneliness that can have a long-term negative impact on a person’s choices regarding relationships and intimate partners.

The author further describes how emotional loneliness can develop in children:

Emotional Loneliness: Parents who are emotionally immature are so self-preoccupied that they don’t notice their children’s inner experiences. In addition, they discount feelings, and they fear emotional intimacy. They’re uncomfortable with their own emotional needs and therefore have no idea how to offer support at an emotional level. Such parents may even become nervous and angry if their children get upset, punishing them instead of comforting them. These reactions shut down children’s instinctive urge to reach out, closing the door to emotional contact.

For some people, emotional loneliness is their default state, but it doesn’t have to be that way. It’s possible to transcend your pain and arrive at a place of secure emotional intimacy, which the author defines as:

Emotional Intimacy: [This] involves knowing that you have someone you can tell anything to, someone to go to with all your feelings, about anything and everything. You feel completely safe opening up to the other person, whether in the form of words, through an exchange of looks, or by just being together quietly in a state of connection. Emotional intimacy is profoundly fulfilling, creating a sense of being seen for who you really are.

So, if you are someone with deep emotional loneliness, how do you find and foster true emotional intimacy?

The remainder of this essay seeks to answer that question by examining the science of attachment theory, and by reviewing a variety of helpful therapeutic techniques (supplemented with examples from my own journey of healing from avoidant attachment).

For me, my deep inner loneliness likely developed from my parents’ neglect of my emotional needs.

My father traveled half the time for work, and when he was home, I had to deal with his occasional anger issues. Even when he was in a good mood, he preferred spending his free time in front of the TV watching the NFL and college basketball—attempts to connect with my father were frequently interrupted by him shouting, “Oh c’mon ref, that’s a bullshit call!” Through repeated experiences, I internalized that my emotional needs would not be met, so I kept to myself, locked myself in my room, and numbed my loneliness by watching YouTube all day.

As a stay-at-home mom, my mother was wonderful and caring. But during my adolescence she returned to work and had less time for me. And in the free time she did have, looking back in retrospect, I don’t think she had ever developed the interpersonal skills to be able to relate to me on an emotional level. Instead, our conversations were mostly about our daily surface-level experiences, rather than helping me navigate life’s emotional challenges. Again, through repeated experiences, I internalized that my emotional needs would not be met, so I isolated myself further and my inner loneliness grew.

As an aside: no parents are perfect. Mine provided for me physically and financially, and I am grateful for that. In many ways, my parents did a way better job raising me compared to their parents, so I don’t want to blame them for anything. When we become adults, it’s up to us to recognize that we now have the power to educate ourselves, become aware of our patterns, redefine our relationships with people (ie: parents, partners, and friends), ask for what we want to feel emotionally fulfilled, and learn to draw boundaries around behaviors that make us uncomfortable.

As a child you have no power, no idea how the world works, or what’s considered normal/healthy. If you happen to grow up in an emotionally insecure home, you have no choice but to adapt.

By numbing myself, I was able to avoid feeling my deep loneliness, but that strategy had unintended consequences later in life…

Deactivating strategies

Once into adulthood and starting to date, my original childhood strategy to avoid emotional neglect and rejection—by isolating and numbing myself—started manifesting through avoidant attachment behaviors, described in the book Attached:

Avoidants … feel a deep-rooted aloneness, even while in a relationship. Whereas people with a secure attachment style find it easy to accept their partners, flaws and all, to depend on them, and to believe that they’re special and unique—for avoidant people such a stance is a major life challenge. If you’re avoidant, you connect with romantic partners but always maintain some mental distance and an escape route. Feeling close and complete with someone else—the emotional equivalent of finding a home—is a condition that you find difficult to maintain.

The emotional and cognitive escape routes that people with avoidant attachment use are known as deactivating strategies:

A deactivating strategy is any behavior or thought that is used to squelch intimacy. These strategies suppress our attachment system, the biological mechanism in our brains responsible for our desire to seek closeness.

Here are some classic deactivating strategies from the book:

  • Saying (or thinking) “I’m not ready to commit”—but staying together nonetheless, sometimes for years
  • Focusing on small imperfections in your partner and allowing it to get in the way of your romantic feelings
  • Pining after an ex-partner
  • Flirting with others—a hurtful way to introduce insecurity into the relationship
  • Not saying “I love you”—while implying that you do have feelings towards the other person
  • Pulling away when things are going well
  • Leaving things foggy—to maintain your feeling of independence
  • Avoiding physical closeness—e.g., not wanting to have sex, walking several strides ahead of your partner

Unfortunately, I’ve used nearly all of the above strategies in my past relationships. It caused my partners to doubt my commitment to them, and to question their self-worth.

Today looking back, I feel ashamed for how I acted, and deeply regret the pain I unintentionally inflicted. Back then, I wasn’t aware of attachment theory, and I was just doing my best to connect with people (while subconsciously avoiding confronting the abyss of emotional loneliness at my core).

Healing from avoidant attachment

First of all, what causes a person with avoidant attachment to become aware of their patterns and to change their behavior? The authors explain:

People with an avoidant attachment style overwhelmingly assume that the reason they’re unable to find happiness in a relationship has little to do with themselves and a lot to do with external circumstances—meeting the wrong people, not finding “the one”. They rarely search inside themselves for the reason of their dissatisfaction, and even more rarely seek help or even agree to get help when their partner suggests they do so. Unfortunately, until they look inward or seek counseling, change is not likely to occur.

On occasions when avoidants reach a low point in their life—because of severe loneliness, a life-altering experience, or a major accident—they can change their way of thinking. 

Yep, what caused me to recognize my avoidant patterns was a difficult breakup.

Take note [that healing from avoidant attachment will] require, first and foremost, increasing your self-awareness. But knowing about the thought patterns that deny you the ability to truly get close to someone is only the first step. The next and harder step requires you to start to identify instances in which you employ these attitudes and behaviors, and then to embark on the voyage of change.

Avoidant attachment strategies manifest in two primary ways to get you to disengage from emotional intimacy and closeness:

  1. Negative emotions (e.g., anxiety, dread, anger, etc.) that can feel overwhelming and can cause you to walk away from intimate moments.
  2. Thought patterns that psychologically justify distancing yourself from someone you’re becoming attached to.

Let’s examine what these look like in the beginning stages of a relationship.

When first starting to date someone, one barrier to intimacy for people is known (in Gen-Z parlance) as “the ick”. When people say they got “the ick” on a date, it means their partner did or said something so unsavory that it turned them off completely. Some icks are universally considered bad:

  • Being rude to waiters.
  • Acting stingy.
  • Poor communication.

But for people with avoidant attachment, insignificant imperfections can be amplified in their mind to justify not getting emotionally close to someone:

  • “They eat pizza with a fork and knife. I could never be with someone like that!”
    • Healthy response: Albeit weird…this doesn’t affect someone’s relationship skills.
  • “They're too emotional all the time!”
    • Healthy response: People have emotional needs and this is normal for relationships.
  • “Their [insert physical feature] isn’t small [or big] enough.”
    • Healthy response: People are allowed to have physical preferences, but it’s good to remember that a perfect body doesn’t exist.

These perceived ‘imperfections’ can trigger negative emotions or deactivating thoughts, which make it more likely that an emotional attachment is never formed in the first place.

If the relationship somehow continues, the person with avoidant attachment will likely develop new thoughts that justify maintaining emotional distance from their partner.

When I used to have avoidant attachment, my mind would constantly invent reasons why a relationship would never work. When I would begin feeling emotionally close and vulnerable with a partner, my anxiety would spike and, without being consciously aware of what was happening, I would employ deactivating strategies to escape. My childhood strategy—isolating and numbing myself to avoid neglect and rejection—was covertly directing all my thoughts and emotions to try to protect me.

Once you’ve become aware of your deep loneliness and your maladaptive present-day patterns (which is usually done via therapy, reading books, and self-reflection), you can then change your behavior by learning and applying the following skills.

  1. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) — Feelings are not problems that need to be solved. Feelings just want to be felt. So if we compulsively avoid negative feelings, like anxiety, we unintentionally make them stronger. But when we relax and sit in uncomfortable feelings, they get felt, processed, and then usually go away.
  2. Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) — If we voluntarily expose ourselves to experiences that give us anxiety, and we prevent a response by refusing to perform avoidant behaviors, we train ourselves to tolerate the disturbing feeling. We learn that while the feeling of anxiety is unpleasant, it's not going to kill us.
  3. Metacognitive Therapy (MCT) — Just like feelings, thoughts also like to be acknowledged and not suppressed. MCT suggests that we observe deactivating thoughts, and then label them non-judgmentally until they go away.
  4. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) — We can identify an avoidant thought, weigh the evidence for whether it’s actually true, and replace it with a more realistic version.


The following is how I healed my attachment style.

During intimate moments, I became acutely aware of the anxiety in my chest, and then said the emotionally vulnerable thing anyway (ACT). After repeatedly choosing to endure the discomfort of intimacy, the intensity of my negative feelings decreased until they went away entirely (ERP).

For me, telling a woman that I loved her for the first time was immensely stressful (my brain screamed, “What if she rejects me?!”), but eventually saying that I love someone began to feel normal.

As for my deactivating thoughts, I began labeling them (MCT) or cognitively restructuring them (CBT). Over time, they also decreased in frequency.

How long does it take to heal from avoidant attachment?

The available research provides a wide timeline. Some people take years to heal, others only need a few months. It depends on how self-aware you are, the overall state of your emotional and mental health, and the amount of effort you dedicate to work on it.

By the time I learned about avoidant attachment, fortunately, across the previous three years, I had already spent thousands of hours developing strong metacognitive skills and emotional regulation, had established deep/intimate relationships with friends, and had already greatly improved my relationship with my parents (who are considered our original attachment figures).

When I began deliberately working on my avoidance, my anxiety around expressing intimacy went away fairly quickly, so I assumed victory!

"Human beings are works in progress that mistakenly think they are finished." - Daniel Gilbert

The avoidant thoughts, however, lingered for quite a while. But I continued using MCT and CBT to label and restructure them until they went away, too. Eventually, rather than just being able to occasionally show up in intimate moments, my emotional availability and expression became consistent.

The total time it took me to make significant progress—split between educating myself, making a list of my emotional and thought patterns, and practicing expressing intimacy with new romantic partners—was about 2-3 months. And progress steadily improved thereafter with continued effort to understand my patterns and replacing them with healthy behaviors.

What a healthy relationship looks like

It’s important to note that the lack of avoidant patterns does not automatically foster a healthy relationship. To become a securely attached partner, the authors from the book Attached recommend you do the following with your partner:

  • Be available: Respond sensitively to their distress, allow them to be dependent on you when they feel the need, check in with them from time to time, and provide comfort when things go wrong.
  • Don’t interfere: Provide behind-the-scenes support for their endeavors. Help in a way that leaves them with the initiative and the feeling of power.
  • Encourage: Provide encouragement and be accepting of their learning and personal growth goals.

In addition to those, the authors also recommend you develop a skill called effective communication:

Don’t be afraid to express your needs, thoughts, and feelings to your partner! What often happens when we’re dating is that we censor ourselves for different reasons: we don’t want to sound too eager or needy or we believe it’s too soon to raise a certain topic. However, expressing your needs and true feelings can be a useful litmus test of the other person’s capacity to meet your needs.

If you have avoidant attachment, being vulnerable and expressing yourself can trigger intense negative emotions and deactivating thoughts. But if you want to heal, that’s exactly what you have to do. You have to tolerate the discomfort in order to transition from your norm of emotional loneliness, to the much healthier place of emotional intimacy.

Two last concepts important for healing from avoidant attachment are: betrayal and trust.

If you are currently in a relationship and have acted avoidantly towards your partner, or looking to rekindle a previous relationship that ended due to your avoidant behavior, take note of this description from the book What Makes Love Last:

Betrayal is the secret that lies at the heart of every failing relationship—it is there even if the couple is unaware of it. Pervasive coldness, selfishness, [and] unfairness are evidence of disloyalty and can lead to consequences as equally devastating as adultery.

Rather than turning towards your partner and establishing emotional intimacy, people with avoidant attachment unintentionally betray their partners by not emotionally committing to them.

This is unacceptable.

Amends need to be made, apologies issued, and long-term behavior change demonstrated in order to establish the next concept, trust:

Trust removes an enormous source of stress because it allows you to act with incomplete information. You don’t subject your mind and body to constant worry, so the complexity of your decision making plummets.

Trust is not some vague quality that grows between two people. It is the specific state that exists when you are both willing to change your own behavior to benefit your partner. The more trust that exists in a relationship, the more you look out for each other. You have your beloved’s back, and vice versa.

On the topic of emotional avoidance, the authors lament:

Over the years I have seen too many people turn away from their partner and toss out a good relationship.
